# How to read this book {.unnumbered #how-to}

::: {.book-hero}

**Hung-Fu Chang, Ph.D. and Wenhui Zhu, Ph.D.**

:::

This book teaches JavaScript in the order a young game designer needs it. Instead of memorizing programming rules first, you will meet a problem inside a game and learn the programming idea that solves it.

Each part is a milestone of your understanding of using JavaScript to build a game.

Chapter 1 prepares your computer and project files. [Chapter 2: Design and develop a game](chapters/02-game-design.qmd) starts with a game story and plans feature-by-feature iterations of Structure → Style → Behavior. Then build one small scene in three gradual lessons: [Chapter 3: Structure](chapters/03-scene-structure.qmd), [Chapter 4: Style](chapters/04-scene-style.qmd), and [Chapter 5: Behavior](chapters/05-game-behavior.qmd). Try each chapter’s examples and exercises before continuing to JavaScript in Chapter 6. The [HTML/CSS reference](appendices/f-html-css-reference.qmd) keeps the detailed catalog available for later lookup.


## Study guide: Concept (READ) → Code → Exercise {.unnumbered}

Use this three-step process for each new topic. Work through one concept at a time before moving to the next.

1. **Concept (READ):** Read the explanation and study the diagrams. Identify the problem the idea solves, then explain the idea in your own words. Before running the example, predict what it will do.
2. **Code:** Type the example into the appropriate project file and run it. Compare the result with your prediction. Trace how the code uses the concept, then change one small thing and observe what happens.
3. **Exercise:** Try the related exercise or challenge on your own. Use the concept to plan your solution, write the code, and test the result. Explain why your solution works. If you get stuck, reread the concept and revisit the example, then try again.

Repeat **Concept (READ) → Code → Exercise** throughout the chapter. For game-building tasks, use **Structure → Style → Behavior** to organize your work during the Code and Exercise steps.

## Choose your reading path {.unnumbered}

Chapters 1-15 establish the web and JavaScript foundations. Chapters 16-19 build a complete 2D adventure. Chapters 20-23 introduce Three.js, custom 3D models, and Rapier physics. The later projects take more time and combine earlier ideas; work through them in small experiments.

Purple **Advanced Study** blocks are optional deeper dives into HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and game systems. They start open; you can collapse them while following the main path and return later.

## Read examples carefully {.unnumbered}

A **complete example** includes the setup for that small project. A **code fragment** illustrates one part of a game and relies on the variables or functions discussed nearby. Do not paste every fragment into one file without checking where it belongs: some examples replace earlier versions.

Chapters 12–14 use Pong, Breakout, and Snake to explain larger game-building patterns. Each chapter includes a complete small browser example alongside fragments explaining individual rules. Locate its scene, its style, and its actions before changing a fragment. Chapters 16-23 add complete companion projects in the Game Lab. Their chapter snippets explain selected parts; the linked project folders contain the complete runnable source.

## A safe learning habit {.unnumbered}

When a program does not work, do not immediately replace it with someone else's code. Read the browser console, compare one small section at a time, and explain what you expected to happen. Debugging is part of programming, not evidence that you failed.

## Open the Game Lab {.unnumbered}

The companion Game Lab contains six complete projects, including two experimental labs, two collectible adventures, a 3D exploration game, and a model-customization workshop. Keep the project folders together so their shared code and assets can be found.

::: {.callout-tip .setup title="Run the later projects" icon="false"}
From the extracted textbook folder, run `node scripts/serve.mjs`. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/` in your browser. This local server needs Node.js but no package installation. Use the [Game Lab guide](appendices/e-game-lab.qmd) for controls, file locations, and troubleshooting.

The 2D projects use local files only. The 3D projects initially download pinned Three.js and Rapier modules from a CDN, so they need an internet connection and a browser with WebGL2. An optional dependency-download script supports later offline use.
:::
